# How East Sussex compares

```{r profile-table}
#| tbl-cap: "East Sussex, Brighton and Hove and England, 2024/25. Means of school-level figures, as in the Lever report; ranks are among all local authorities (1 = highest)."
row <- function(lab, col, d = 1) {
  f <- function(x) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
  rnk <- function(p) sprintf("%s (%s)", f(p[[col]]), ord(rank(-prof[[col]])[prof$LANAME == p$LANAME]))
  tibble(Measure = lab, `East Sussex` = rnk(p_es), `Brighton and Hove` = rnk(p_bh),
         England = f(mean(prof[[col]] * prof$schools, na.rm = TRUE) /
                       mean(prof$schools[!is.na(prof[[col]])])))
}
bind_rows(
  row("Attainment 8, all pupils", "att8"),
  row("Attainment 8, disadvantaged", "att8_dis"),
  row("Attainment 8, non-disadvantaged", "att8_non"),
  row("Disadvantage gap (points)", "gap"),
  row("Disadvantaged (FSM6) %", "fsm"),
  row("Overall absence %", "absence"),
  row("Persistent absence %", "persistent"),
  row("Mean KS2 (centred)", "ks2_c", 2),
  row("EAL %", "eal"),
  row("EHC plan %", "sen_ehcp")) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

Three features stand out against England:

- **Lower attainment for every group.** The shortfall is widest for
  disadvantaged pupils, so the county's disadvantage gap is among the
  widest fifth in England.
- **Lower prior attainment.** Pupils arrive from primary school with
  lower Key Stage 2 scores than the national average. The national model
  treats this as one of the two strongest predictors of results at 16.
- **Higher absence, but not higher disadvantage.** The county's schools
  are less disadvantaged than the national average and less than
  Brighton and Hove's. Its absence is high.

```{r trend}
#| fig-cap: "Attainment 8 for disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils, school means, 2021/22 to 2024/25. England is the mean over all schools."
#| fig-height: 4.8
nat_y <- ES$profiles |>
  group_by(year_label) |>
  summarise(att8_dis = weighted.mean(att8_dis, schools, na.rm = TRUE),
            att8_non = weighted.mean(att8_non, schools, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(LANAME = "England")
ES$profiles |>
  filter(LANAME %in% c(FOCUS, COMP)) |>
  select(year_label, LANAME, att8_dis, att8_non) |>
  bind_rows(nat_y) |>
  pivot_longer(c(att8_dis, att8_non), names_to = "grp", values_to = "att8") |>
  mutate(grp = recode(grp, att8_dis = "Disadvantaged pupils", att8_non = "Non-disadvantaged pupils"),
         LANAME = factor(LANAME, c(FOCUS, COMP, "England"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year_label, att8, colour = LANAME, group = LANAME)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~grp, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Attainment 8",
       title = "The county trails England for both groups, every year") +
  theme_note()
```

# What explains attainment in East Sussex {#sec-decomp}

The national model predicts a school's Attainment 8 from its intake and
circumstances. Averaged over a local authority's schools, those
predictions add up exactly to the authority's average result, piece by
piece. That makes it possible to ask how much of the gap between East
Sussex and England each factor accounts for:

- the county's absence against England's;
- its prior attainment against England's;
- and so on through every other term.

The pieces add up to the whole gap. Anything the model's factors do not
cover lands in the last bar, labelled "unexplained", and for East Sussex
it is small.

```{r fig-decomp}
#| fig-cap: "Why average Attainment 8 differs from England's, by factor, all school-years 2021/22 to 2024/25. Bars to the left pull the area below England; bars to the right lift it. The pieces sum to the total gap printed in each panel. Approximate Attainment 8 points."
#| fig-height: 7.5
comp_order <- c("Absence", "Prior attainment (KS2)", "Disadvantage (% FSM)",
                "English as an additional language", "Admissions (selection)",
                "Segregation (LA)", "Teacher workforce", "Ofsted rating",
                "Region", "Local authority effect", "Year mix",
                "Unexplained (school residual)")
lab <- dec |> distinct(la, group, la_att8, nat_att8) |>
  mutate(la = factor(la, c(FOCUS, COMP)),
         txt = sprintf("%.1f vs England %.1f\ntotal %+.1f", la_att8, nat_att8, la_att8 - nat_att8))
dec |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, rev(comp_order)),
         la = factor(la, c(FOCUS, COMP)),
         dir = ifelse(points < 0, "Pulls below England", "Lifts above England")) |>
  ggplot(aes(points, component, fill = dir)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  # Rows 6 to 8 (workforce, segregation, admissions) are short in every
  # panel, so the total sits there without covering a bar
  geom_label(data = lab, aes(x = Inf, y = 7, label = txt), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             hjust = 1.02, size = 2.9, colour = INK, fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
  facet_grid(la ~ group) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Pulls below England" = BAD, "Lifts above England" = TEAL), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Approximate Attainment 8 points", y = NULL,
       title = "What separates each area's results from England's",
       subtitle = "Each bar is one factor's contribution to the difference") +
  theme_note(11) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

```{r decomp-table}
#| tbl-cap: "The same decomposition for East Sussex, in Attainment 8 points. Region and local authority are shown together as 'place'."
dec |>
  filter(la == FOCUS) |>
  mutate(component = case_when(component %in% c("Region", "Local authority effect") ~ "Place (region and local authority)",
                               component %in% c("Segregation (LA)", "Year mix", "Admissions (selection)") ~ "Other model terms",
                               TRUE ~ component)) |>
  group_by(group, component) |> summarise(points = sum(points), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = points) |>
  arrange(`All pupils`) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~sprintf("%+.2f", .x))) |>
  rename(Factor = component) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

**For all pupils**, East Sussex is
`r pts(-d_tot(FOCUS, "All pupils"))` points below England. Almost all of
that is two factors of roughly equal size:

- **absence** (`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2)`);
- **prior attainment** (`r pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Prior attainment (KS2)"), 2)`).

Lower Ofsted ratings and a low share of pupils with English as an
additional language take a little more. Place nets out at about zero:
the South East's negative regional effect is offset by the county's own
small positive one.

**For disadvantaged pupils** the gap is
`r pts(-d_tot(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged"))` points, and the picture
changes in two ways:

- **Place matters much more.** Across England, disadvantaged pupils
  outside London do worse than the model's other factors predict, and the
  South East is one of the regions where that is most marked. Place takes
  `r pts(-(d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "Region") + d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "Local authority effect")), 2)`
  points, nearly as much as absence
  (`r pts(-d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "Absence"), 2)`).
- **English as an additional language takes more.** East Sussex's
  disadvantaged pupils are rarely from the multilingual families whose
  children do well nationally
  (`r pts(-d_get(FOCUS, "Disadvantaged", "English as an additional language"), 2)`).

Neither is something the county can change. Absence and prior
attainment are the two pieces it can.

**What does not appear** is just as informative. Concentrations of
disadvantage contribute almost nothing, and if anything work in the
county's favour, because its schools are less disadvantaged than
England's. The segregation index contributes nothing. Teacher workforce
measures contribute little. Nothing here suggests that the mix of pupils
between schools is what holds East Sussex back.

**The contrast with Brighton and Hove is the clearest thing in the
chart.** Absence costs Brighton and Hove *more* than it costs East
Sussex (`r pts(-d_get(COMP, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2)` points against
`r pts(-d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2)`), and its pupils arrive
with *higher* prior attainment. What lifts the city above England is
its local authority effect: its schools get more out of their pupils
than the model predicts (+`r pts(d_get(COMP, "All pupils", "Local authority effect"), 2)`
points). East Sussex has neither the city's prior-attainment advantage
nor its school effect. That leaves absence as the largest single
addressable factor.

# The county's own effect

Once intake and circumstances are accounted for, each local authority's
schools sit somewhere above or below the national expectation. This is
the local authority random effect in the model, plotted for every
authority in @fig-caterpillar.

```{r fig-caterpillar}
#| fig-cap: "Local authority effects from the published national models, disadvantaged pupils. Each dot is an authority, ordered by estimate, with a 95% interval. East Sussex is teal; Brighton and Hove pink."
#| fig-height: 5.5
cd <- eff |> filter(group == "Disadvantaged") |>
  mutate(hl = case_when(la == FOCUS ~ FOCUS, la == COMP ~ COMP, TRUE ~ "Other"),
         la_o = reorder(la, effect))
ggplot(cd, aes(la_o, effect)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi, colour = hl == "Other"), width = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = hl == "Other"), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = filter(cd, hl != "Other"), aes(fill = hl), shape = 21, size = 3.5, colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = GREY) +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(cd, hl != "Other"), aes(label = la), size = 3.4, nudge_y = 0.06,
                  segment.colour = GREY) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = LIGHT, `FALSE` = LIGHT), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = AREA_COL, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Local authorities, ordered", y = "Effect (log scale; 0.01 is about 1%)",
       title = "East Sussex's schools perform close to the national expectation") +
  theme_note() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

```{r tbl-effects}
#| tbl-cap: "Local authority effects and ranks (1 = best). 'Significant' means the 95% interval excludes zero."
eff |> filter(la %in% c(FOCUS, COMP)) |>
  transmute(Group = group, `Local authority` = la,
            `Effect (%)` = sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (exp(effect) - 1)),
            Rank = sprintf("%s of %d", ord(rank), n_las),
            Significant = ifelse(sig, "Yes", "No")) |>
  arrange(Group, `Local authority`) |>
  kt(align = "llrrl")
```

East Sussex ranks `r ord(e_es("All pupils")$rank)` for all pupils,
`r ord(e_es("Disadvantaged")$rank)` for disadvantaged pupils and
`r ord(e_es("Non-disadvantaged")$rank)` for non-disadvantaged pupils. In
each case it is slightly above the middle, worth about
`r pp(100 * (exp(e_es("All pupils")$effect) - 1))`% on Attainment 8, and
in none is it distinguishable from average. **The county's schools,
taken together, get about the results the national model expects for
pupils like theirs, in a place like theirs.**

**Does that depend on controlling for absence?** For Brighton and Hove it
depends on it entirely, and this was one of the central findings of the
Lever report:

- with the absence control, the city ranks
  `r ord(r27("dis", COMP, "A-raw"))` for disadvantaged pupils;
- without it, `r ord(r27("dis", COMP, "A-none"))`.

The city's schools are effective for the pupils who attend, and the
city's absence erases the advantage. For East Sussex the control makes
almost no difference: `r ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-raw"))` with it,
`r ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-none"))` without.[^r27] The county's absence
is not hiding unusually effective schools. It is at about the level its
intake predicts (@sec-intake), so taking it out of the model moves the
county very little.

[^r27]: These two ranks come from the peer-review re-estimation in the
Lever report, fitted on a common sample so that the two specifications
can be compared. They differ slightly from the published model's ranks
in the table above for that reason.

## Do the districts differ? {#sec-districts}

```{r district-setup}
#| include: false
DE <- readRDS(here::here("data", "district_effects.rds"))
tst <- function(o, s) DE$tests |> filter(outcome == o, spec == s)
vsd <- function(o, s, lvl) DE$vcs |> filter(outcome == o, spec == s, grepl(lvl, level)) |> pull(sd)
pct <- function(x) 100 * (exp(x) - 1)
SPEC0 <- "Published specification"; SPEC1 <- "With a school term"
fe <- function(o, s, l) DE$focus |> filter(outcome == o, spec == s, lad == l)
ev <- DE$every |> filter(n_lad > 1)
n_sig <- function(o, s) sum(ev$sig[ev$outcome == o & ev$spec == s])
n_dist <- function(o, s) sum(ev$outcome == o & ev$spec == s)
dva <- DE$es_va |> group_by(lad) |> summarise(n = n(), va = mean(va), .groups = "drop")
se_h <- DE$school_eff |> filter(lad == "Hastings")
se_at <- function(o, s) pct(se_h$school_effect[se_h$outcome == o & grepl(s, se_h$SCHNAME)])
```

The published models place schools in local authorities within regions.
In a two-tier county that skips a level. East Sussex is five districts
and boroughs with very different towns in them, and it is fair to ask
whether those districts carry an effect of their own.

**The test.** To find out, a district level is added to the published
model, nested inside the local authority, and the model is refitted with
and without it on identical school-years. This is done for all three
attainment outcomes and for the first-stage absence model. Every school
in England was placed in its district from its postcode. In a unitary
authority the district is the authority, so the district variance is
estimated from the two-tier counties: `r n_dist("All pupils", SPEC0)`
districts in all.

**The catch.** The published models have no term for the individual
school. A school that does persistently well or badly across its four
years therefore has nowhere to go but the lowest place level in the
model. When a district has only three schools, as Hastings does, a
"district effect" is largely those three schools. So the test is run
twice: once on the published specification, and once with a school term
added, which asks whether the district matters *beyond* the schools in
it.

```{r tbl-district-tests}
#| tbl-cap: "Does adding a district level improve the model? Likelihood-ratio tests (the p-value is halved because a variance cannot be negative), with the district standard deviation alongside the local authority's. A standard deviation of 0.02 is about 2% of Attainment 8, or of the absence rate."
DE$tests |>
  left_join(DE$vcs |> filter(grepl("^lad", level)) |> select(outcome, spec, sd_lad = sd), by = c("outcome", "spec")) |>
  left_join(DE$vcs |> filter(level == "LANAME:gor_name") |> select(outcome, spec, sd_la = sd), by = c("outcome", "spec")) |>
  transmute(Specification = spec, Outcome = outcome,
            `LR statistic` = sprintf("%.1f", lrt),
            p = ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p)),
            `BIC prefers` = ifelse(bic1 < bic0, "District", "No district"),
            `District SD` = sprintf("%.3f", sd_lad), `LA SD` = sprintf("%.3f", sd_la)) |>
  kt(align = "llrrlrr")
```

**Nationally, districts matter, but much less once schools are counted.**
On the published specification the district level is overwhelmingly
significant for every outcome. Districts within a county differ by more
than counties do from each other: the district standard deviation is
`r sprintf("%.3f", vsd("All pupils", SPEC0, "^lad"))` for all pupils,
against `r sprintf("%.3f", vsd("All pupils", SPEC0, "^LANAME"))` for the
local authority.

With a school term most of that goes. A district effect survives for all
pupils and, more clearly, for non-disadvantaged pupils. For
disadvantaged pupils and for absence it is marginal (p =
`r sprintf("%.2f", tst("Disadvantaged", SPEC1)$p)` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", tst("Absence (stage 1)", SPEC1)$p)`), and the BIC
prefers the model without it. Of the `r n_dist("All pupils", SPEC1)`
county districts, `r n_sig("All pupils", SPEC1)` have an individually
significant effect on attainment once schools are counted, and
`r n_sig("Absence (stage 1)", SPEC1)` on absence.

```{r fig-districts}
#| fig-cap: "East Sussex's five districts: the district effect on Attainment 8 (all pupils and disadvantaged) and on absence, with 95% intervals, before and after adding a school term. Effects are percentages of the outcome over and above the county's own effect. For absence, positive means more absence than intake predicts."
#| fig-height: 5.6
DE$focus |> filter(la == FOCUS) |>
  mutate(spec = factor(spec, c(SPEC0, SPEC1)),
         outcome = factor(outcome, c("All pupils", "Disadvantaged", "Non-disadvantaged", "Absence (stage 1)")),
         lad = factor(lad, rev(sort(unique(lad))))) |>
  filter(outcome != "Non-disadvantaged") |>
  ggplot(aes(pct(effect), lad, colour = spec)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pct(ci_lo), xmax = pct(ci_hi)), height = 0,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 2.6) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(WARM, TEAL), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "District effect, %", y = NULL,
       title = "Hastings and Lewes stand out until the schools are counted") +
  theme_note()
```

**In East Sussex the districts' differences are their schools.** On the
published specification two districts stand out. Hastings sits
`r pp(-pct(fe("All pupils", SPEC0, "Hastings")$effect))`% below
expectation for all pupils and runs
`r pp(pct(fe("Absence (stage 1)", SPEC0, "Hastings")$effect))`% more
absence than its intake predicts. Lewes sits
`r pp(pct(fe("All pupils", SPEC0, "Lewes")$effect))`% above. Eastbourne
runs `r pp(-pct(fe("Absence (stage 1)", SPEC0, "Eastbourne")$effect))`%
*less* absence than predicted.

A plain comparison of the county's 26 schools says the same: value
added differs by district (F = `r sprintf("%.1f", DE$aov_va[["F value"]][1])`,
p = `r sprintf("%.2f", DE$aov_va[["Pr(>F)"]][1])`). That comparison runs
from Hastings at `r pts(dva$va[dva$lad == "Hastings"])` points a pupil to
Lewes at `r sprintf("%+.1f", dva$va[dva$lad == "Lewes"])`.

With a school term, every one of those district effects is
indistinguishable from zero. Hastings' attainment effect falls to
`r pp(pct(fe("All pupils", SPEC1, "Hastings")$effect))`% and its absence
effect to `r sprintf("%+.1f", pct(fe("Absence (stage 1)", SPEC1, "Hastings")$effect))`%.
What looked like Hastings was two of its three schools:

- **The St Leonards Academy**: `r pp(se_at("All pupils", "Leonards"))`%
  on attainment and `r sprintf("%+.0f", se_at("Absence (stage 1)", "Leonards"))`%
  on absence, beyond its intake;
- **The Hastings Academy**: `r pp(se_at("All pupils", "Hastings Academy"))`%
  and `r sprintf("%+.0f", se_at("Absence (stage 1)", "Hastings Academy"))`%;
- **Ark Alexandra Academy**, the third school in the same town, is much
  closer to expectation: `r pp(se_at("All pupils", "Alexandra"))`% and
  `r sprintf("%+.0f", se_at("Absence (stage 1)", "Alexandra"))`%.

Lewes' advantage is likewise King's Academy Ringmer, Priory School and
Seahaven Academy, not the district's other three schools.

```{r fig-school-effects}
#| fig-cap: "Each East Sussex school's own persistent effect from the model with a school term, coloured by district: Attainment 8 (all pupils) and absence beyond what its intake predicts. Schools are in the same order in both panels, by their attainment effect."
#| fig-height: 6.2
# Both panels share one order - the attainment effect - so a school sits
# on the same row in each and the two can be read across
att_order <- DE$school_eff |> filter(LANAME == FOCUS, outcome == "All pupils") |>
  arrange(school_effect) |> pull(SCHNAME)
DE$school_eff |> filter(LANAME == FOCUS) |>
  filter(outcome %in% c("All pupils", "Absence (stage 1)")) |>
  mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, c("All pupils", "Absence (stage 1)"),
                          c("Attainment 8, all pupils (%)", "Absence beyond intake (%)")),
         SCHNAME = factor(SCHNAME, att_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct(school_effect), SCHNAME)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = pct(school_effect), yend = SCHNAME), colour = LIGHT) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = lad), size = 2.6) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "School effect, %", y = NULL,
       title = "The district pattern is a handful of schools at each end") +
  theme_note(11)
```

**What this means for the county.**

- **District is a useful way to describe where the difficulties are.**
  Hastings has the county's most disadvantaged intakes and two of the
  county's three lowest-performing schools.
- **It is not, on this evidence, a separate cause.** The model finds no
  sign that being in Hastings, Eastbourne or Lewes affects a school's
  results or attendance beyond what its intake and its own record
  explain. A district-wide intervention would be aimed at an effect the
  data cannot find, where school-level support would be aimed at one it
  can.
- **The limit of the test.** With three to six schools per district,
  four years of data cannot fully separate a shared place effect from
  several schools that happen to sit together. The two Hastings
  academies have also moved to the same trust together, so what they
  share is governance as well as geography. A place effect smaller
  than the school differences could exist and go undetected.

## Do trusts make a difference? {#sec-trusts}

```{r trust-setup}
#| include: false
tt  <- function(o) TR$tests |> filter(outcome == o)
tsd <- function(o, l) TR$vcs |> filter(outcome == o, level == l) |> pull(sd)
rte <- function(o, r) TR$routes |> filter(outcome == o, term == r)
es_trusts <- unique(GOV$run_by[GOV$trust_kind == "Multi-academy trust"])
TE <- TR$trusts |>
  mutate(name = tidy_trust(trust_group)) |>
  filter(name %in% es_trusts)
te_at <- function(n, o) TE |> filter(name == n, outcome == o)
nsig <- function(o, s) sum(TR$trusts$outcome == o & TR$trusts$sig & sign(TR$trusts$effect) == s)
```

Many of the county's schools are in multi-academy trusts, so it is
natural to ask whether a trust carries an effect of its own, like a
district might. Do schools in the same trust do better or worse together
than their pupils and places would predict?

**How it is tested.** The trust is added to the national model as
another grouping level, crossed with the local authority, since many
trusts span several. Three choices make the test fair to trusts:

- **The trust that actually ran the school that year.** Membership comes
  from the DfE's school-level exclusions file, which names each school's
  trust year by year. A school's results before it joined a trust are
  never credited to that trust.
- **Each school's own record is in the model too**, so a trust is not
  credited or blamed for the persistent strengths of one school.
- **How each school came to be run enters as a fixed effect.** Its route
  is maintained, converter academy, sponsored academy or free school.
  This is the point about selection. Sponsored academies were usually
  placed with a trust *because* they were struggling, so a trust that
  takes on such schools would look worse for reasons that are not its
  doing. Comparing like with like on route removes the crudest version of
  that bias.

The trust term applies only to school-years in a multi-academy trust.
Maintained schools and single-academy trusts carry none.

```{r tbl-trust-tests}
#| tbl-cap: "Does adding the trust improve the national model? Likelihood-ratio test (p-value halved for the boundary), with the standard deviations of the trust, local authority and school effects. 0.02 is about 2% of Attainment 8, or of the absence rate."
TR$tests |>
  transmute(Outcome = outcome, `LR statistic` = sprintf("%.0f", lrt),
            p = ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p)),
            `BIC prefers` = ifelse(bic1 < bic0, "Trust", "No trust"),
            `Trust SD` = sapply(outcome, function(o) sprintf("%.3f", tsd(o, "trust_group"))),
            `LA SD` = sapply(outcome, function(o) sprintf("%.3f", tsd(o, "LANAME:gor_name"))),
            `School SD` = sapply(outcome, function(o) sprintf("%.3f", tsd(o, "URN")))) |>
  kt(align = "lrrlrrr")
```

**Schools in the same trust do share something.** The trust level is
strongly significant for every outcome, and the model is better with it
on every criterion. Its size is the useful number:

- **All pupils.** A trust moves Attainment 8 by about
  `r pp(100 * tsd("All pupils", "trust_group"))`% either way, the same as
  the local authority does
  (`r pp(100 * tsd("All pupils", "LANAME:gor_name"))`%). The individual
  school moves it by
  `r pp(100 * tsd("All pupils", "URN"))`%, about three times as much.
- **Disadvantaged pupils.** The trust matters more,
  `r pp(100 * tsd("Disadvantaged", "trust_group"))`% against
  `r pp(100 * tsd("Disadvantaged", "LANAME:gor_name"))`% for the local
  authority.
- **Absence.** The trust matters most:
  `r pp(100 * tsd("Absence (stage 1)", "trust_group"))`% of the absence
  rate, beyond intake, against
  `r pp(100 * tsd("Absence (stage 1)", "LANAME:gor_name"))`% for the local
  authority.

**But few individual trusts can be told apart from average.** Of
`r TR$n_mats` trusts in England:

- **All pupils:** `r nsig("All pupils", 1)` are significantly above
  average and `r nsig("All pupils", -1)` below.
- **Disadvantaged pupils:** `r nsig("Disadvantaged", 1)` above and
  `r nsig("Disadvantaged", -1)` below.
- **Absence:** `r nsig("Absence (stage 1)", 1)` run significantly more
  absence than their schools' intakes predict, and
  `r nsig("Absence (stage 1)", -1)` less.

Most trusts are small, and a trust of two or three schools cannot be
separated from the schools themselves.

```{r tbl-route}
#| tbl-cap: "How a school came to be run, compared with maintained schools of the same intake, place and Ofsted rating: percentage difference in Attainment 8, and in absence beyond what the intake predicts."
TR$routes |>
  filter(outcome %in% c("All pupils", "Disadvantaged", "Absence (stage 1)")) |>
  mutate(v = sprintf("%+.1f%% (t = %.1f)", 100 * (exp(estimate) - 1), t)) |>
  select(term, outcome, v) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = v) |>
  rename(Route = term) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

The route shows the selection problem directly. Compared with maintained
schools with the same intake, sponsored academies have
`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (exp(rte("Absence (stage 1)", "Sponsor-led academy")$estimate) - 1))`%
more absence than predicted and
`r sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (exp(rte("All pupils", "Sponsor-led academy")$estimate) - 1))`%
lower attainment. These schools were sponsored because they were in
difficulty. Their histories cannot be separated from what their trusts
have done since. The data do not say that sponsorship causes absence.
They say that the schools trusts are given are harder, in ways the
intake measures do not fully capture.

```{r fig-trusts}
#| fig-cap: "The national effect of each trust that ran an East Sussex school in 2024/25, with 95% intervals: Attainment 8 for all pupils and for disadvantaged pupils, and absence beyond intake (positive means more absence). Each trust's effect is estimated across all its secondary schools in England, not only its East Sussex ones; the number in brackets is how many it has in the data."
#| fig-height: 6
TE |>
  filter(outcome %in% c("All pupils", "Disadvantaged", "Absence (stage 1)")) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s (%d)", name, schools_in_data),
         outcome = factor(outcome, c("All pupils", "Disadvantaged", "Absence (stage 1)")),
         sigc = ifelse(sig, "Distinguishable from average", "Not distinguishable")) |>
  group_by(label) |> mutate(o = effect[outcome == "All pupils"][1]) |> ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(100 * (exp(effect) - 1), reorder(label, o), colour = sigc)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = 100 * (exp(ci_lo) - 1), xmax = 100 * (exp(ci_hi) - 1)), height = 0) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Distinguishable from average" = WARM,
                                 "Not distinguishable" = TEAL), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Trust effect, %", y = NULL,
       title = "Two of the county's trusts stand out nationally; most are close to average") +
  theme_note(11)
```

```{r trust-names}
#| include: false
ul <- function(o) te_at("United Learning Trust", o)
ark <- function(o) te_at("Ark Schools", o)
ub <- function(o) te_at("University of Brighton Academies Trust", o)
pc <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * (exp(x$effect) - 1))
```

The trusts that ran East Sussex schools in 2024/25 span the range, and
two stand out nationally.

- **United Learning**, which runs Seahaven Academy, is among the
  strongest trusts in England. Across its `r ul("All pupils")$schools_in_data`
  secondary schools in the data, results are `r pc(ul("All pupils"))`%
  above what their intakes predict, and `r pc(ul("Disadvantaged"))`% for
  disadvantaged pupils. Seahaven's own record matches this
  (@fig-governance).
- **Ark Schools**, which runs Ark Alexandra Academy in Hastings, is
  significantly better than average for disadvantaged pupils
  (`r pc(ark("Disadvantaged"))`%). Its schools run
  `r sub("^-", "", pc(ark("Absence (stage 1)")))`% *less* absence than
  their intakes predict, among the strongest attendance records of any
  trust.
- **The University of Brighton Academies Trust** ran The Hastings and St
  Leonards academies until 2025/26. Its national effect is
  `r pc(ub("All pupils"))`% on attainment and `r pc(ub("Absence (stage 1)"))`%
  on absence, neither distinguishable from average. With so few schools
  in the data, it cannot be separated from the two Hastings schools
  themselves (@sec-districts).
- **The county's small local trusts** (Seaford, South Downs, Cavendish
  and Mark) sit at about zero. With one or two schools each, that is
  what the model must report. Their trust and their school are the same
  thing, and the school's own effect carries the difference.

**What this means for the county.** Trusts are a real level in the
system, about as consequential as the local authority itself. They
matter more for disadvantaged pupils and attendance than for results
overall. Ark's attendance record and United Learning's attainment are
national strengths with a school in the county, and both are worth
learning from. But for most trusts the evidence cannot say whether they
are better or worse than average. It cannot say whether the county's
academies would do better under the council, or the council's schools
under a trust. The strongest effect in the model remains the individual
school.

# Absence in East Sussex {#sec-absence}

## Ten years of secondary absence

```{r fig-abs-series}
#| fig-cap: "Overall absence in state-funded secondary schools, autumn and spring terms, 2016/17 to 2025/26. Sessions-weighted. 2019/20 was not collected."
#| fig-height: 5
ser |>
  mutate(year = yr(time_period), area = factor(area, names(AREA_COL))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, abs_rate, colour = area, group = area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Overall absence, % of sessions",
       title = "East Sussex has run above England for a decade, and is now closing the gap") +
  theme_note() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r tbl-abs-ranks}
#| tbl-cap: "Secondary absence and persistent absence (10% or more of sessions missed), autumn and spring terms, with rank among local authorities (1 = highest absence)."
rk |> filter(la_name %in% c(FOCUS, COMP)) |>
  transmute(Year = yr(time_period), la_name,
            v = sprintf("%.1f%% (%s) / %.1f%% (%s)", abs_rate, ord(rank_abs), pa_rate, ord(rank_pa))) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = la_name, values_from = v) |>
  left_join(ser |> filter(area == "England") |>
              transmute(Year = yr(time_period),
                        England = sprintf("%.1f%% / %.1f%%", abs_rate, pa_rate)), by = "Year") |>
  rename(`East Sussex: absence / persistent` = all_of(FOCUS),
         `Brighton and Hove` = all_of(COMP)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

Absence in East Sussex was high long before the pandemic. In 2016/17
and 2017/18 the county was the 9th highest of over 150 authorities,
alongside Brighton and Hove. Like everywhere, absence roughly doubled
after the pandemic. The county peaked at `r pp(s_at(FOCUS, "202223"))`%
in `r yr("202223")` (`r ord(rk_at(FOCUS, "202223"))` highest), and has
improved every year since, to `r pp(s_at(FOCUS, abs_last))`% in
`r yr(abs_last)` (`r ord(rk_at(FOCUS, abs_last))`). Over the same years
England fell by
`r pp(s_at("England", "202223") - s_at("England", abs_last))` points and
Brighton and Hove by
`r pp(s_at(COMP, "202223") - s_at(COMP, abs_last))`. East Sussex's
improvement is real and faster than average, but the county is still
`r pp(gap_tot)` points above England.

## Is it the intake? {#sec-intake}

Absence is partly a property of the pupils a school serves. Lower prior
attainment, disadvantage and a lack of English as an additional language
all predict higher absence across England. The first stage of the Lever
report's absence decomposition fits that relationship nationally, using
intake and region but not the local authority. It then asks how far each
authority's absence is above or below what its intake predicts.

```{r fig-intake}
#| fig-cap: "Each local authority's mean school absence (2021/22 to 2024/25) against the absence its intake predicts. Authorities above the line have more absence than their intake explains."
#| fig-height: 5.5
ctx2 <- ctx |> mutate(hl = case_when(LANAME == FOCUS ~ FOCUS, LANAME == COMP ~ COMP, TRUE ~ "Other"))
ggplot(ctx2, aes(mean_exp_abs_NoL, mean_abs)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = GREY, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = filter(ctx2, hl == "Other"), colour = LIGHT, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = filter(ctx2, hl != "Other"), aes(fill = hl), shape = 21, size = 4, colour = "white") +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(ctx2, hl != "Other"), aes(label = LANAME), size = 3.6, nudge_x = -0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = AREA_COL, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Absence predicted by intake, %", y = "Actual absence, %",
       title = "Brighton and Hove's absence is far above its intake; East Sussex's is close to it") +
  theme_note()
```

East Sussex's intake predicts high absence: `r pp(c_es$mean_exp_abs_NoL)`%,
against `r pp(c_bh$mean_exp_abs_NoL)`% for Brighton and Hove's. Actual
absence is `r pp(c_es$mean_abs)`%, only `r pp(c_es$excess, 2)` points
above that (`r ord(c_es$rank_excess)` of `r c_es$n_las`). Brighton and
Hove's intake predicts low absence, and its actual absence is
`r pp(c_bh$excess)` points above that, the `r ord(c_bh$rank_excess)` largest
excess in England.

This is the sharpest difference between the two authorities.

- **Brighton and Hove's absence is a local anomaly.** It has the absence
  of a much more deprived place without the deprivation. That points to
  local causes, which is why the Lever report recommended a dedicated
  study.
- **East Sussex's absence is the national pattern, at the level its
  intake produces everywhere.** It has the pupils who are absent most
  across England: lower prior attainment, little English as an
  additional language, and coastal deprivation.

That is not a reason for fatalism. "Predicted by intake" means "typical
of schools with intakes like this", and typical is still a lot of
absence. Schools with similar intakes vary widely (@sec-plane). The
county's improvement since 2022/23 shows the rate can move. But the
levers are likely to be the ones that work nationally for these pupils,
rather than a search for something unusual about East Sussex.

## What the absence is {#sec-reasons}

Every absent session is recorded against a reason.
@fig-reasons compares East Sussex's profile with England's and Brighton
and Hove's, as a share of all possible sessions.

```{r fig-reasons}
#| fig-cap: "Absence by register reason, autumn and spring terms, state-funded secondary schools, percentage of possible sessions. The ten largest reasons nationally."
#| fig-height: 5.2
top <- rs_w |> arrange(desc(England)) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> pull(reason)
rs |> filter(reason %in% top) |>
  mutate(reason = factor(reason, rev(top)), area = factor(area, c(FOCUS, COMP, "England"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pp, reason, fill = area)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% of possible sessions", y = NULL,
       title = paste("Illness and unauthorised absence account for most of it,", yr(abs_last))) +
  theme_note()
```

```{r tbl-reason-gap}
#| tbl-cap: "Where East Sussex's excess over England comes from, by reason, in percentage points of possible sessions. The rows sum to the total gap."
rs_gap |>
  filter(abs(gap) >= 0.01) |>
  transmute(Reason = reason, `East Sussex` = sprintf("%.2f", .data[[FOCUS]]),
            England = sprintf("%.2f", England), Gap = sprintf("%+.2f", gap),
            `Share of gap` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * gap / gap_tot)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrr")
```

East Sussex is `r pp(gap_tot, 2)` points above England in
`r yr(abs_last)`, and three reasons make up the excess:

- **Illness**, `r pp(gap_of("Illness"), 2)` points: about
  `r pp(100 * gap_of("Illness") / gap_tot, 0)`% of the gap.
- **Unauthorised absence**, `r pp(gap_of("Unauthorised, other"), 2)`
  points. This is the category that covers truancy and absence the
  school does not accept.
- **Reduced timetables**, `r pp(gap_of("Reduced timetable"), 2)` points.
  These are pupils formally attending part-time, often while a placement
  or support is arranged. The figure is small but notable, because it
  reflects decisions made within the system rather than by families.

Unauthorised holidays are at the national rate and late arrival is
below it. Suspension adds only `r pp(gap_of("Suspended (code E)"), 2)`.

The same is true of Brighton and Hove, more strongly. The Lever
report's companion note on exclusions found that illness was 95% of the
city's excess. Neither authority's problem is mainly holidays, lateness
or exclusion. Both are mainly pupils recorded as ill, and in East Sussex
also pupils absent without permission.

## Within the county

```{r fig-within}
#| fig-cap: "School absence against disadvantage, East Sussex, 2024/25, coloured by district. The dotted line is England's school average absence."
#| fig-height: 6.5
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = S, aes(fsm, absence, fill = district), shape = 21, size = 3.5, colour = "white") +
  geom_text_repel(data = S, aes(fsm, absence, label = SCHNAME), size = 2.8,
                  max.overlaps = 30, segment.colour = LIGHT) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = NAT$absence, linetype = "dotted", colour = GREY) +
  annotate("text", x = max(S$fsm), y = NAT$absence, vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1,
           label = sprintf("England school average %.1f%%", NAT$absence), size = 3, colour = GREY) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Disadvantaged pupils (FSM6), %", y = "Overall absence, %",
       title = "Absence rises with disadvantage, but schools with similar intakes differ by several points") +
  theme_note()
```

Disadvantage and absence go together within the county, as they do
nationally. But at any level of disadvantage there is a spread of three
or four points between schools. Two examples:

- The Cavendish School and Ark Alexandra Academy are both a quarter to a
  third disadvantaged. They differ by more than two points of absence.
- Priory School in Lewes, one of the county's less disadvantaged
  schools, has higher absence than five of the six Eastbourne schools.

That spread is where school practice shows. @sec-plane separates it from
intake more formally.

## Suspensions {#sec-suspensions}

```{r fig-susp}
#| fig-cap: "Suspensions per 100 pupils, state-funded secondary schools, full academic years."
#| fig-height: 4.6
bind_rows(ex_la |> filter(la_name %in% c(FOCUS, COMP)) |> select(time_period, la_name, susp_rate),
          ES$excl$england |> select(time_period, la_name, susp_rate)) |>
  filter(time_period >= "201617") |>
  mutate(year = yr(time_period), la_name = factor(la_name, c(FOCUS, COMP, "England"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, susp_rate, colour = la_name, group = la_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Suspensions per 100 pupils",
       title = "East Sussex suspends at well above the national rate") +
  theme_note() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Suspensions rose sharply everywhere after the pandemic, and further in
East Sussex. The county's rate peaked at
`r pp(ex_at(FOCUS, "202324"))` per 100 pupils in `r yr("202324")`
(`r ord(ex_at(FOCUS, "202324", "rank_susp"))` highest of
`r ex_at(FOCUS, "202324", "n_la")`). In `r yr(ex_last)` it was
`r pp(ex_at(FOCUS, ex_last))`, against `r pp(ex_eng(ex_last))` for England
and `r pp(ex_at(COMP, ex_last))` for Brighton and Hove. Permanent
exclusion, by contrast, is *below* the national rate:
`r pp(ex_at(FOCUS, ex_last, "perm_rate"), 2)` per 100 against
`r pp(ex_eng(ex_last, "perm_rate"), 2)`.

```{r tbl-susp-schools}
#| tbl-cap: "Suspensions and permanent exclusions by school, latest year. A rate is suspensions per 100 pupils on roll; one pupil can be suspended more than once."
ES$excl_schools |>
  filter(!is.na(susp_rate)) |>
  arrange(desc(susp_rate)) |>
  transmute(School = school_name, Pupils = headcount,
            `Suspensions per 100` = round(susp_rate, 1),
            `Permanent exclusions` = perm_excl) |>
  kt(align = "lrrr")
```

The rate varies enormously between schools, and that variation is the
real policy question about suspensions in the county. For absence they
are a small part of the story. Sessions lost to suspension are
`r pp(rs_w[[FOCUS]][rs_w$reason == "Suspended (code E)"], 2)`% of possible
sessions in `r yr(abs_last)`, about
`r pp(100 * rs_w[[FOCUS]][rs_w$reason == "Suspended (code E)"] / s_at(FOCUS, abs_last), 0)`%
of all absence. A county with England's suspension rate would have
almost exactly the absence East Sussex has. Suspension is worth
attention for what it does to the pupils suspended, who are
disproportionately disadvantaged and have special educational needs. It
is not the reason the county's absence is high.

# What absence costs, school by school

## Two signals: what a school adds, and how it manages attendance {#sec-plane}

The Lever report separates each school's absence into two parts:

- the part its intake predicts;
- the residual, which is broadly what the school's own attendance
  practice adds or removes.

It sets the residual against a value-added measure that does *not*
control for absence. That measure gives schools credit for attendance
they have improved, and charges them for attendance they have not.
@fig-plane places every East Sussex school on those two axes, against
the national cloud. These are the two models refitted for this document,
both exact copies of the Lever report's.

```{r fig-plane}
#| fig-cap: "East Sussex schools on the joint-signal plane, mean over 2021/22 to 2024/25. Horizontal: absence above (right) or below (left) what the intake predicts. Vertical: Attainment 8 above or below what the intake predicts, with attendance counted as part of the school's contribution. Grey: every school in England."
#| fig-height: 7
xl <- quantile(js$resid_abs_pp, c(0.005, 0.995)); yl <- quantile(js$vadd_M2, c(0.005, 0.995))
xl <- c(min(xl[1], -4), max(xl[2], 4.5)); yl <- c(min(yl[1], -8), max(yl[2], 9))
ggplot(js, aes(resid_abs_pp, vadd_M2)) +
  geom_point(colour = LIGHT, size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = GREY) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_point(data = js_es, fill = TEAL, shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 3.6) +
  geom_text_repel(data = js_es, aes(label = SCHNAME), size = 2.8, max.overlaps = 40,
                  segment.colour = GREY, colour = INK) +
  annotate("text", x = xl[1], y = yl[2], hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3, colour = TEAL,
           label = "Adds value, attendance\nbetter than intake predicts") +
  annotate("text", x = xl[2], y = yl[2], hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 3, colour = WARM,
           label = "Adds value despite\nworse attendance") +
  annotate("text", x = xl[2], y = yl[1], hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = BAD,
           label = "Below expectation,\nattendance worse") +
  annotate("text", x = xl[1], y = yl[1], hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = PURPLE,
           label = "Below expectation despite\nbetter attendance") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = xl, ylim = yl) +
  labs(x = "Absence above what the intake predicts (percentage points)",
       y = "Value added, attendance counted in (Attainment 8 points)",
       title = "Attendance and attainment go together school by school") +
  theme_note()
```

```{r plane-q}
#| include: false
q <- js_es |> mutate(q = case_when(vadd_M2 >= 0 & resid_abs_pp < 0 ~ 1, vadd_M2 >= 0 ~ 2,
                                   resid_abs_pp >= 0 ~ 3, TRUE ~ 4))
qn <- function(k) paste(q$SCHNAME[q$q == k], collapse = ", ")
r_cor <- cor(js_es$resid_abs_pp, js_es$vadd_M2)
```

Across the county's schools the two signals are strongly related
(correlation `r sprintf("%.2f", r_cor)`). Schools that hold attendance
better than their intake predicts also tend to add more to results.

- **Better attendance and value added.** `r qn(1)`.
- **Value added despite worse attendance.** `r qn(2)`. In these schools
  attendance is the obvious next lever.
- **Below expectation, with worse attendance.** `r qn(3)`. Here both
  signals point the same way. The Hastings and St Leonards academies,
  Rye College and the Turing School are furthest out.
- **Below expectation despite better attendance.**
  `r if (nzchar(qn(4))) paste0(qn(4), ". These are the hardest cases for any authority, because the gap is not attendance.") else "No East Sussex school is in this quadrant. Every school below expectation also has worse attendance than its intake predicts, which makes attendance the common thread."`

Two cautions apply.

- **Some of the residual is not the school's doing.** About half of
  national absence is explained by intake. The rest includes local
  health, transport and family circumstances that a school can influence
  only partly.
- **These are four-year averages.** Several of the schools furthest from
  the centre have changed leadership or trust since.

## What closing the gap would be worth

The Lever report's scenario asks what each school would gain if its
absence fell to the national school average of
`r pp(NAT$absence)`%. The model's absence coefficient converts the fall
into Attainment 8 points. The Lever report also works through the
alternative lever: bringing each school's disadvantage down to the
county average.

```{r tbl-scenario}
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted Attainment 8 gain if each school's absence fell to the national school average (2024/25), and, for comparison, if its disadvantage fell to the county average. Schools already at or below either target gain nothing from it. Indicative only: see the cautions in the Lever report."
sc |>
  filter(gain_all > 0 | gain_fsm > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(gain_all)) |>
  transmute(School = SCHNAME, District = district,
            `Absence %` = round(absence, 1), `FSM %` = round(fsm, 1),
            `Gain, all pupils` = sprintf("%+.1f", gain_all),
            `Gain, disadvantaged` = sprintf("%+.1f", gain_dis),
            `Gain from FSM to county average` = sprintf("%+.1f", gain_fsm)) |>
  kt(align = "llrrrrr")
```

`r nrow(sc_above)` of the county's `r nrow(sc)` schools are above the
national average. At the highest-absence schools the predicted gain is
three to four Attainment 8 points: The Turing School, Seahaven Academy,
Priory School, Rye College and Robertsbridge Community College. Across
all `r nrow(sc_above)`, the average is
`r pts(mean(sc_above$gain_all))` points for all pupils and
`r pts(mean(sc_above$gain_dis, na.rm = TRUE))` for disadvantaged pupils,
whose results respond more to attendance.

The disadvantage lever buys very little by comparison: at most
`r pts(max(sc$gain_fsm))` points, at the schools with the highest
concentrations. The county's schools do not have extreme concentrations
of disadvantage, and the model gives concentration a small coefficient.
In East Sussex, as the Lever report found for Brighton and Hove,
attendance is the lever with the mechanical advantage.

```{r fig-returns}
#| fig-cap: "Predicted Attainment 8 gain from a one-point reduction, at each starting level: absence (solid) and disadvantage (dashed). Returns grow as each falls, reading right to left. East Sussex schools marked on each curve."
#| fig-height: 5.3
b_fsm <- ES$coefs$all[["log(PTFSM6CLA1A)"]]; b_abs <- ES$coefs$all[["log(PERCTOT)"]]
base <- mean(S$att8)
curve <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = seq(5, 55, 0.5), Variable = "% FSM (disadvantaged)", b = b_fsm),
  tibble(x = seq(4, 16, 0.1), Variable = "% absence", b = b_abs)) |>
  mutate(gain = base * (exp(b * (log(x - 1) - log(x))) - 1))
dots <- bind_rows(
  S |> transmute(SCHNAME, x = fsm, Variable = "% FSM (disadvantaged)", b = b_fsm),
  S |> transmute(SCHNAME, x = absence, Variable = "% absence", b = b_abs)) |>
  mutate(gain = base * (exp(b * (log(x - 1) - log(x))) - 1))
ggplot(curve, aes(x, gain, colour = Variable, linetype = Variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = dots, size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("% FSM (disadvantaged)" = PURPLE, "% absence" = TEAL), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("% FSM (disadvantaged)" = "dashed", "% absence" = "solid"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Current level (%)", y = "Attainment 8 gain from a 1-point reduction",
       title = "A point of absence is worth several points of disadvantage") +
  theme_note()
```

# School by school: contextual league tables

A raw league table mostly ranks intakes. The contextual tables below
rank schools on how far their results sit above or below what the
national model expects, given their pupils' disadvantage, prior
attainment, absence and the rest. This is the measure the Lever report
uses for Brighton and Hove. The 2025/26 column is provisional, from the
first release of that year's results.

```{r va-tables}
#| include: false
va_tab <- function(col) {
  ES$va |> filter(LANAME == FOCUS) |>
    select(school, year_label, v = all_of(col)) |>
    filter(!is.na(v)) |>
    group_by(school) |> mutate(Mean = mean(v), Years = n()) |> ungroup() |>
    mutate(year_label = sub("-", "/", year_label)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = year_label, values_from = v) |>
    arrange(desc(Mean)) |>
    relocate(Mean, Years, .after = last_col())
}
fmt_va <- function(t) {
  num <- names(t)[sapply(t, is.numeric) & names(t) != "Years"]
  t |> mutate(across(all_of(num), ~ifelse(is.na(.x), "", sprintf("%+.1f", .x)))) |>
    rename(School = school)
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## All pupils

```{r va-all}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added, all pupils: observed Attainment 8 minus the national model's expectation, in points. Schools ordered by their mean."
fmt_va(va_tab("va_ATT8SCR")) |> kt(align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 7)))
```

## Disadvantaged pupils

```{r va-dis}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added, disadvantaged pupils. These are smaller groups, and a school's figure can move by several points from year to year."
fmt_va(va_tab("va_ATT8SCR_FSM6CLA1A")) |> kt(align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 7)))
```

## Non-disadvantaged pupils

```{r va-non}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added, non-disadvantaged pupils."
fmt_va(va_tab("va_ATT8SCR_NFSM6CLA1A")) |> kt(align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 7)))
```

:::

```{r va-notes}
#| include: false
vt <- va_tab("va_ATT8SCR")
vt_d <- va_tab("va_ATT8SCR_FSM6CLA1A")
top3 <- head(vt$school, 3)
bot3 <- tail(vt$school, 3)
```

The county has schools at both ends of the national distribution:

- **At the top on all pupils:** `r paste(top3, collapse = ", ")`. These
  schools consistently get more from their pupils than the model
  expects.
- **At the bottom:** `r paste(bot3, collapse = ", ")`. These are
  consistently below expectation, and are the schools where trust and
  leadership have since changed.

The disadvantaged table re-orders the middle considerably.
`r vt_d$school[1]` is first for disadvantaged pupils, and some schools
with solid overall figures are well below expectation for their
disadvantaged pupils. Two examples are Chailey School and Gildredge
House. Priory School is strongly positive overall and negative for its
disadvantaged pupils. Differences like these are where a conversation
with the schools themselves would add most.

# East Sussex and Brighton and Hove

The two authorities are neighbours on the same coast, and some pupils
cross the boundary between them each day. On the headline measures they
look alike: absence well above England's, near-average disadvantage, and
a disadvantage gap of about fifteen points. The model says they are
quite different.

```{r tbl-contrast}
#| tbl-cap: "The two authorities side by side. Absence and suspension figures are the latest DfE releases; model figures are from the national models over 2021/22 to 2024/25."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Measure, ~`East Sussex`, ~`Brighton and Hove`,
  "Attainment 8, all pupils (2024/25)", pts(p_es$att8), pts(p_bh$att8),
  "Attainment 8, disadvantaged (2024/25)", pts(p_es$att8_dis), pts(p_bh$att8_dis),
  "Disadvantaged %", pp(p_es$fsm), pp(p_bh$fsm),
  "Prior attainment (KS2, centred)", pp(p_es$ks2_c, 2), pp(p_bh$ks2_c, 2),
  paste("Absence,", yr(abs_last), "(rank)"),
    sprintf("%.1f%% (%s)", s_at(FOCUS, abs_last), ord(rk_at(FOCUS, abs_last))),
    sprintf("%.1f%% (%s)", s_at(COMP, abs_last), ord(rk_at(COMP, abs_last))),
  "Absence above intake-predicted (rank)",
    sprintf("%+.2f (%s)", c_es$excess, ord(c_es$rank_excess)),
    sprintf("%+.2f (%s)", c_bh$excess, ord(c_bh$rank_excess)),
  "Illness, % of possible sessions",
    pp(rs_w[[FOCUS]][rs_w$reason == "Illness"], 2), pp(rs_w[[COMP]][rs_w$reason == "Illness"], 2),
  paste("Suspensions per 100,", yr(ex_last)),
    pp(ex_at(FOCUS, ex_last)), pp(ex_at(COMP, ex_last)),
  "LA effect, all pupils (rank)", ord(e_es("All pupils")$rank), ord(e_bh("All pupils")$rank),
  "LA effect, disadvantaged (rank)", ord(e_es("Disadvantaged")$rank), ord(e_bh("Disadvantaged")$rank),
  "Disadvantaged rank: with / without absence control",
    paste(ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-raw")), "/", ord(r27("dis", FOCUS, "A-none"))),
    paste(ord(r27("dis", COMP, "A-raw")), "/", ord(r27("dis", COMP, "A-none"))),
  "Absence's cost to the gap with England (points, all pupils)",
    pts(d_get(FOCUS, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2), pts(d_get(COMP, "All pupils", "Absence"), 2)) |>
  kt(align = "lrr")
```

- **Brighton and Hove** has effective schools, an advantaged intake and
  a local absence problem out of all proportion to its intake. Absence is
  the one thing standing between the city and the top of the national
  table. The policy question there is diagnostic: *why* is attendance so
  much worse than the city's pupils would predict?
- **East Sussex** has schools that perform about as the model expects,
  pupils who arrive with lower prior attainment, and absence that is high
  but roughly what its intake predicts. Absence is still the largest
  factor the county can act on, but it is not an anomaly. The policy
  question is about delivery: how to move a typical, intake-driven
  attendance problem in places where it is concentrated, chiefly the
  coastal towns and a handful of schools.
- **What they share** is the composition of the problem. In both, most of
  the excess is pupils recorded as ill, not holidays, lateness or
  exclusion. In neither does the mix of pupils between schools explain
  attainment. Both would get more from attendance than from any
  redistribution of disadvantage.
- **Where they differ most sharply apart from that** is suspension. East
  Sussex suspends at more than twice Brighton and Hove's rate. That is
  not a large part of either authority's absence, but it is a large
  difference in practice between two neighbours.

# Implications and questions for discussion

These are offered as starting points for the conversation with the
county. They are not recommendations made with knowledge of what the
county already does.

1. **Attendance is the largest factor the county can act on.** It
   accounts for as much of the attainment gap with England as prior
   attainment does. The gain per point is largest in the
   highest-absence schools, and largest for disadvantaged pupils.
2. **The county's absence is the national problem, concentrated.**
   Approaches that work for pupils with lower prior attainment, in
   coastal and rural areas with poor transport, are likely to transfer.
   The improvement since 2022/23 suggests something is already working.
   It would be worth knowing what, and in which schools.
3. **Illness is most of the excess.** Illness absence above the
   national rate, here and in Brighton and Hove, is beyond what schools
   alone can address, and points to joint work with health and
   children's services. The published data cannot say what lies behind
   it; the county's own attendance records could.
4. **Reduced timetables and suspensions are system decisions.** Both run
   above national rates. Neither is large in absence terms, but both fall
   on the pupils least able to absorb lost time, and both are within the
   system's control.
5. **Prior attainment is the other half of the gap.** Pupils arriving
   with lower Key Stage 2 scores account for as much of the county's
   shortfall as absence does. The primary phase is part of the secondary
   story.
6. **Hastings.** The Hastings and St Leonards academies have the
   lowest value added in the county, with absence well above what their
   intakes predict, and both have just changed trust. The
   value-added and attendance measures in this document give a baseline
   against which the new arrangements could be followed.

**What would sharpen this.** All of the following are published or
routinely collected by the county:

- attendance by year group and pupil characteristic for each school;
- persistent and severe absence by reason;
- the use of reduced timetables and alternative provision;
- the primary schools that feed each secondary.

Any of these would allow the school-level picture here to be taken
further.

# Notes on method {.unnumbered}

**The decomposition.** For a model fitted on log Attainment 8, a
school-year's outcome is the sum of its fixed-effect terms (coefficient
times predictor), its random effects (year, Ofsted rating, region, local
authority) and a residual. Averaging over an authority's school-years
and subtracting England's average gives the gap in log points as an
exact sum of one term per factor. Each term is converted to approximate
Attainment 8 points by multiplying by England's geometric mean Attainment
8. The pieces are computed on the school-years each model was fitted on,
so the three groups cover slightly different sets.

**Absence.** Absence rates in @sec-absence are sessions-weighted across
pupils, from the DfE's school-level release for autumn and spring terms.
They differ slightly from the school-mean rates in the model tables,
which weight every school equally.

**Sources.** DfE school performance tables 2021/22–2024/25 and Key stage 4
performance 2025/26 (provisional); Pupil absence in schools in England;
Suspensions and permanent exclusions in England; School workforce in
England; Get Information about Schools. All are published under the Open
Government Licence v3.0. The models and code are at
<https://github.com/adamdennett/school_attainment_tool>; this document
is built by `R/17_east_sussex.R` and `east_sussex.qmd`.
